category.name: Tradecraft & OPSEC
category.description: Tools for protecting the investigator and the integrity of the investigation: separating research identity from personal identity, encrypting what you hold, capturing evidence defensibly, and knowing where to look next. The subject of an investigation is not the only person at risk in one.

tools.name: Tor Browser
tools.summary: Hardened browser routing traffic through the Tor network to separate your research from your identity and location.
tools.description:
Tor Browser routes traffic through a volunteer relay network so the sites you visit do not learn your real address, and hardens the browser itself against fingerprinting so that your session is not distinguishable from other Tor users.

The research use is straightforward. Visiting a target's website from your newsroom's address tells that target you are looking, and for a small site with attentive logs it can identify your organisation before you publish. Tor removes that signal. It is also the only way to reach onion services, which matters for research into markets, leak sites and forums.

The limits are as important as the capability. Tor protects the network layer only: logging into an account, filling a form or enabling a plugin identifies you regardless. Exit-node traffic is unencrypted to the destination unless the site uses HTTPS. Many sites block or degrade Tor. And in some jurisdictions Tor use is itself monitored or restricted, so it can be a signal rather than a shield — in those places bridges and pluggable transports exist for exactly this reason. Never assume Tor makes you anonymous; it makes your network path anonymous, and everything else is still up to you.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source, developed by the non-profit Tor Project. No account.
tools.legalNotes: Lawful in most jurisdictions, but restricted, blocked or treated as suspicious in some — check your local position and that of any country you are working from. Using Tor to access material that is unlawful to access does not make it lawful. Note that Tor protects your network path and does nothing about what you disclose through your behaviour: one login to a personal account over a Tor circuit undoes it.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The network works as designed and is well studied, but it is a network-layer tool and users routinely over-trust it. Browser fingerprinting, behavioural correlation, timing analysis by a sufficiently capable adversary, and simple operator error are all real. Slower than a normal connection, and widely blocked or CAPTCHA-walled, which pushes users toward exactly the shortcuts that break their protection.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established non-profit project. Not fetched during this review. Always download from the official project site and verify the signature.

tools.name: Tails
tools.summary: Amnesic live operating system that boots from USB, routes everything through Tor and leaves no trace on the machine.
tools.description:
Tails is a Debian-based live operating system you boot from a USB stick. All network traffic is forced through Tor, and unless you deliberately configure encrypted persistent storage, nothing is written to disk — on shutdown the session is gone, including from the host machine's drives.

It exists for the situations where a compromised or merely untrusted working machine is the threat. Journalists handling source material, researchers working in hostile environments, and anyone who needs a clean environment that cannot retain traces use it because it removes a whole class of forensic exposure. It ships with the tools that go with that posture: encrypted storage, a password manager, secure deletion, GPG and messaging.

Limits: it is deliberately inconvenient, and inconvenience is where opsec fails. It requires rebooting into a separate environment, hardware compatibility is imperfect, and persistence must be configured deliberately and correctly. It also does not protect against a compromised BIOS or firmware, hardware keyloggers, or an adversary who simply observes that you booted a Tails stick.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source, developed by a non-profit and funded by donations and grants. No account.
tools.legalNotes: Lawful in most jurisdictions, but possession or use of anonymity tools attracts attention in some, and at a border crossing a Tails USB stick may itself invite questions. Assess your threat model, including whether the fact of using it is safe where you are. Tails does not launder the legality of anything you do with it.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Well engineered, security-audited and actively maintained, and it does what it claims. The realistic failure modes are the user's: misconfigured persistence, booting the wrong machine, or reverting to a normal environment for one convenient task. It cannot defend against firmware-level compromise or physical surveillance. Hardware compatibility problems, particularly with wireless adapters, are a recurring practical obstacle.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established project with sustained institutional support. Not fetched during this review. Download only from the official site and verify the image signature — this is a high-value target for supply-chain attack.

tools.name: KeePassXC
tools.summary: Offline, open-source password manager storing credentials in a local encrypted database.
tools.description:
KeePassXC keeps credentials in an encrypted file on your own machine. There is no vendor, no cloud service and no account, which means there is no third party to be breached, subpoenaed, or to observe which services you hold credentials for.

That property is the reason it belongs in an investigator's toolkit specifically. Serious research means many accounts — research personas on platforms, API keys, data-service logins — and the set of services you have accounts with is itself sensitive information that reveals what you are working on. A cloud password manager knows that set. KeePassXC does not, because nobody but you holds the database.

Limits: you are responsible for backing it up and for syncing it yourself if you use multiple machines, and if you lose the master password the data is gone. That is the trade for having no vendor, and it is a real cost that should be planned for rather than discovered.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source under GPL. No account, no subscription, no vendor infrastructure.
tools.legalNotes: Local encryption software. Note that a few jurisdictions have laws compelling disclosure of decryption keys under legal process, and encryption import/export controls exist in a small number of countries — relevant if you travel with an encrypted database. Storing credentials for research personas is fine; storing credentials belonging to someone else is not.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Mature, actively maintained, independently audited, using well-established cryptography and an open file format that other tools can read — which means you are not locked in and can migrate. The reliability burden sits with the user: no vendor means no password recovery and no automatic backup. Set up backups on day one.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established open-source project with an active release cadence. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: VeraCrypt
tools.summary: Open-source disk and container encryption for protecting case files at rest.
tools.description:
VeraCrypt creates encrypted volumes — either a file-backed container or a full encrypted partition or drive — that mount as ordinary drives when unlocked. It is the successor to TrueCrypt and addresses several weaknesses found in that project's audit.

For investigative work its role is straightforward and non-optional: material about identifiable people, source-provided documents and case notes must be encrypted at rest. A laptop is lost or seized, and unencrypted case material at that moment is a data breach involving people who never consented to being in your files. Under GDPR that is a notifiable incident with real consequences; under any ethical standard it is a betrayal of a source.

Use it for the case file, not for the whole workflow. Limits: it protects data at rest only — once a volume is mounted the contents are as exposed as any other file, and an adversary with access to a running machine gets everything. It also does not defend against a compromised operating system, and its hidden-volume feature offers far less real deniability than users imagine, particularly where key-disclosure law applies.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source. No account or licence fee.
tools.legalNotes: Encryption is lawful in most jurisdictions but restricted in a few, and several — including the UK under RIPA and equivalents elsewhere — can compel disclosure of keys under legal process, with criminal penalties for refusal. Hidden volumes do not reliably solve this and may worsen your position. If you travel with encrypted case material, understand the border and key-disclosure position of every country on your route before you go.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Mature, audited and widely used, built on standard cryptographic primitives. Correct use matters more than the software: a weak passphrase defeats it entirely, and a mounted volume is not protected. Full-disk encryption is generally the better default for a working machine, with VeraCrypt containers for specific material that must stay sealed separately.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established open-source project with continued releases. Not fetched during this review; verify downloads against the project's published signatures.

tools.name: Hunchly
tools.summary: Browser extension that silently captures every page you visit during an investigation, building a timestamped, hashed evidence trail.
tools.description:
Hunchly runs in the background while you work and captures every page you visit into a case file: the full page content, a screenshot, the URL, a timestamp, and a cryptographic hash of the capture. It also tracks selectors you define and flags when they appear on a page you visit.

It solves the problem that ruins otherwise good investigations. You find something important, you move on, and by the time you write it up the page has changed or gone — and you have a screenshot with no provenance. Hunchly captures continuously and automatically, so you have the evidence whether or not you realised at the time that you needed it. The hashing and timestamping give you a chain of custody you can actually defend, which matters if your work goes to a court, a regulator or a rigorous editor.

It is a paid product and the only one in this category, which is worth stating plainly. It is also, for professional casework, close to unmatched at what it does.

Limits: it captures what your browser renders, so authenticated sessions and personal accounts get captured too — use a dedicated research browser profile. Storage grows quickly. And it records your process, which is exactly what you want when your work is scrutinised and exactly what you must think about if your case file could be compelled.
tools.costNotes: Commercial software sold as an annual per-seat licence, with volume discounts for multiple licences. Third-party sources report a single-seat annual price in the low hundreds of US dollars, but this was not confirmed against the vendor's own pricing page during this review and no figure is asserted here. A trial has historically been offered.
tools.legalNotes: Captures everything you browse while running, including material unrelated to the case and any personal accounts you use in that browser — run it in a dedicated profile. The resulting case file is a detailed record of your investigative process, which is an asset if your findings are challenged and a liability if the file can be compelled in litigation or by a state actor. Encrypt case files at rest. Captured third-party content remains under its original copyright.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Dependable capture with sound hashing and timestamping, and a well-established reputation in professional investigation. It captures what the browser rendered, so pages that fail to render fully are captured incompletely, and heavily dynamic content can be captured mid-state. Hashes prove the capture has not been altered since; they do not prove the page said what the capture shows at the moment of capture — that rests on your process and, ideally, an independent archive of the same page.
tools.confidenceNotes: The product is real, current and widely used in professional investigation. Its exact pricing was not verified against the vendor's own page, and a secondary source encountered during this review also asserted a change in the product's corporate ownership, which could not be confirmed and is therefore not stated in this entry. Verify both before purchase.

tools.name: HTTrack
tools.summary: Open-source website mirroring tool for preserving an entire site as a browsable local copy.
tools.description:
HTTrack downloads a website recursively and rebuilds it locally as a browsable copy with working internal links. Where the Wayback Machine preserves individual pages, HTTrack preserves a site.

That is the right tool when the whole structure matters — a company site whose subsidiary pages, staff listings and document archive together tell the story, or a site you expect to be taken down entirely. Having a complete local copy means you can search it, diff it against a later capture, and demonstrate what the site contained rather than what one page said.

Using it responsibly is not optional and is the reason this entry carries the warnings it does. HTTrack respects robots.txt by default and provides bandwidth and rate controls. Leave those alone. An unthrottled mirror of a large site is indistinguishable from a denial-of-service attempt from the operator's side, and it is loud — it will be noticed, and it discloses your interest as clearly as a phone call would.

Limits: it handles static sites well and JavaScript-driven applications poorly, often capturing an empty shell.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source under GPL. No account.
tools.legalNotes: This is the tool where this catalogue's robots.txt and rate-limit principle stops being abstract. Respect robots.txt, keep the default rate limits, and identify yourself honestly in the user agent. Aggressive mirroring can degrade a target's service, which moves the act from lawful collection toward conduct that may engage computer-misuse legislation in the UK, the CFAA in the US, and equivalents elsewhere — intent matters less than effect. Terms of service on many sites prohibit mirroring outright. Copyright subsists in the downloaded content and a local copy is not a republication licence. Mirroring is also highly visible in server logs and will alert an attentive target.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Reliable and long-established for conventional server-rendered sites. Modern JavaScript applications frequently mirror as an empty shell because the content is fetched at runtime — check what you actually captured rather than assuming. Sites behind authentication, CDN bot protection or aggressive rate limiting will produce partial mirrors that look complete.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established open-source utility. Not fetched during this review; the project has had long periods between releases.

tools.name: Bellingcat's Online Investigation Toolkit
tools.summary: Bellingcat's curated, maintained directory of open-source investigation tools, organised by task.
tools.description:
Bellingcat maintains a public directory of the tools its researchers actually use, organised by category — satellite and aerial imagery, social media, transport, archiving, maps, geolocation and more — with short notes on what each does and, importantly, on what has stopped working.

It is worth consulting even alongside this catalogue, and this entry says so deliberately. Bellingcat's list reflects the working practice of an organisation doing this at the highest level continuously, it is community-maintained through an open repository, and it turns over faster than any editorially reviewed catalogue can. When something in this catalogue has quietly died, the toolkit is one of the places that will notice first.

Use it as a discovery surface. Its entries are necessarily brief and do not carry the legal, cost and reliability assessment that this catalogue exists to provide, and inclusion there — as here — is not endorsement.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account. Published as a GitBook with an open source repository behind it.
tools.legalNotes: A directory of tools, not a tool. Each listed tool carries its own legal position, which the toolkit does not assess in depth — do not read inclusion as an indication that a tool is lawful in your jurisdiction or appropriate for your purpose.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Well curated by practitioners and updated more frequently than most directories, with an open contribution process. Entries are brief by design and carry no reliability, cost or legal assessment. Like every tool directory including this one, individual entries can be stale — always confirm a tool is live before building a method around it.
tools.confidenceNotes: The canonical URL was confirmed during this review, along with the existence of the backing open source repository and the category structure described.

tools.name: IntelTechniques Search Tools
tools.summary: Michael Bazzell's collection of query-building forms that construct precise searches across many services at once.
tools.description:
The IntelTechniques search tools are a set of web forms, one per category — email, username, domain, telephone, images, maps and others. You enter an identifier once and the page generates correctly formed query links to dozens of relevant services, so you can work through them systematically rather than reconstructing each search by hand.

The value is method as much as convenience. Working through a structured tool page enforces a consistent, repeatable process, which is what makes an investigation defensible and what prevents the common failure of checking three sources, finding something, and stopping. They are maintained as a supplement to the OSINT Techniques book and were last updated on 15 August 2026, which is a good sign of active upkeep in a space where link collections rot fast.

Limits: they are link builders, so every underlying service's own limitations, costs and legal considerations apply unchanged — the page does not vet them. Some generated links will be dead as services change. And clicking through dozens of services in sequence discloses your subject's identifier to every one of them, which is a meaningful cumulative exposure for a sensitive case.
tools.costNotes: Free to use, no account. Maintained as a companion to a commercial book and training offering.
tools.legalNotes: A query-construction aid rather than a data source. Each destination service imposes its own terms, costs and jurisdiction, and none of that is assessed on the page. Be aware that running an identifier through a long sequence of third-party services discloses that identifier to all of them, which is exactly the cumulative footprint you may be trying to avoid in a sensitive investigation.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Well maintained by a long-standing practitioner and updated regularly, most recently in August 2026. Individual generated links break as target services change their URL structures or shut down, and there is no per-link status indication. Reliability of results is entirely that of the destination service.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as live and actively maintained, with an update date of 15 August 2026 and a stated relationship to the current edition of the associated book.
